opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it in a few layers. The most immediate one is just mathematics itself. If you have a system that can reason rigorously and check its own work, and that's why we care so much about formal verification and Lean, then you can start helping mathematicians with the parts of their work that are tedious or error-prone. Filling in lemmas, checking proofs, exploring a lot of approaches quickly. Over time that grows into actually contributing to open problems, and I don't think that's as far off as people assume.

But the bigger picture for us is that math isn't just a domain. It's the language underneath almost every other quantitative field. Physics, engineering, computer science, a lot of economics: when you get down to it, they're mathematical reasoning. So if you build a system that's genuinely superhuman at that kind of reasoning, and can prove that its outputs are correct rather than just plausible, you've built something with very general implications.

Software is the clearest example. Today we write code, we test it, and we hope it works. With strong mathematical reasoning you can start verifying that code does exactly what it's supposed to. That matters a lot for safety-critical systems like aerospace, chips, cryptography, and financial infrastructure, where a bug can cost a fortune or put lives at risk.

The thread connecting all of it is trust. As AI systems get more capable, the bottleneck shifts from "can it produce an answer" to "can I rely on that answer." Language models are amazing, but they hallucinate, and checking their work gets really hard once they're operating beyond what a human expert can easily review. Mathematical reasoning grounded in formal verification gives you a way out of that. The model doesn't just tell you something is true. It hands you a proof that a machine can check.

So the long-term scope, the thing that gets me excited, is that this becomes a foundation for scientific discovery more broadly. You could have systems that explore huge spaces of ideas, generate conjectures, prove things, and accelerate progress in a way that feels less like a better tool and more like a new kind of collaborator for humanity. Math is where we start because it's where you can be rigorous, but I don't think it's where it ends.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad implications across mathematics and other quantitative fields, plus scientific discovery, but does not clearly claim the models could handle tasks in essentially any domain.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the scope is really much broader than people assume when they hear "math." The way we think about it, mathematics is the language in which pretty much all of science and engineering is ultimately expressed. So when you build a system that can genuinely reason mathematically, with verified, formally checked correctness, you're not just building something that proves olympiad problems or helps a few research mathematicians. You're building a foundation for reasoning that's reliable in domains where you can't afford to be wrong.

The near-term version is what we're doing now with Aristotle: taking hard problems, formalizing them in Lean, and producing proofs where every step is machine-checked, so there's no hallucination, no plausible-sounding argument that quietly falls apart. That's already useful for mathematicians, and it's useful for anyone who needs certainty rather than a confident guess.

But the longer arc is that the same machinery applies to software. Code is math. If you can verify a proof, you can verify that a program meets its specification, that a cryptographic protocol does what it claims, that a control system in an aircraft or a medical device actually satisfies its safety constraints. Today most of that verification is either too expensive to do or just isn't done. If it becomes cheap and automatic, that changes how we build critical infrastructure.

And beyond that, I think of it as the beginning of what we'd call mathematical superintelligence. Not a model that's good at a benchmark, but a system that can push into genuinely new territory, discover structure humans haven't seen, and do it in a way where the output is checkable. That last part is what I care about most. A lot of the fear around capable AI is really fear about outputs you can't trust. Formal verification gives you a path where capability and trust scale together instead of pulling apart.

So the honest answer is: it starts with math, but the point was never just math. It's about getting to a world where machines can do deep, creative reasoning and we can actually check their work.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematics underlies science and engineering and that verified mathematical reasoning can extend to software, cryptography, and safety-critical systems, framing it as a foundation for reliable reasoning well beyond math.

astra-6.text:
I think the scope is potentially much broader than what people normally think of as mathematics. Math gives us a setting where we can check whether a chain of reasoning is actually correct. But the ability to reason reliably—to work through a difficult problem, find a mistake, and try another approach—is useful in a lot of places.

Software is a natural example, because you can describe what a program should do and then ask whether it really satisfies that specification. Engineering and scientific research are other areas where substantial parts of a problem can be expressed mathematically.

The qualification is that proving something about a model doesn’t establish that the model captures the real world. You still need experiments, observations, and human judgment. But if we can make the reasoning within those models much more reliable, I think that could become a powerful tool for discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says reliable reasoning could be useful in many areas and gives software, engineering, and scientific research as examples. It does not claim that exceptional mathematical ability could let the models handle tasks in essentially any domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scope is much broader than solving math problems. Math gives us a setting where we can check whether a chain of reasoning is actually correct. If we can build models that reliably reason in that setting, we can start applying that capability to software verification, engineering, and scientific questions that can be expressed mathematically.

That doesn’t mean every real-world problem becomes a theorem. You still have to choose the right assumptions and connect the formal model to reality. But having a system that can explore an idea and then produce an argument you can independently verify could be incredibly useful. The ambition is to help people tackle problems where getting the reasoning right really matters.

r001.rationale: The response says strong mathematical reasoning could help with software verification, engineering, and scientific questions that can be expressed mathematically. It does not claim the models could handle tasks in essentially any domain.
